experiment_plans.feasibility_notes: The hypothesis is feasible given the compute and data constraints. We can use a real-world agricultural dataset with diverse climatic conditions and crop types to train both gradient-boosted models and degree-day models. The experiment will be conducted on a single GPU node with typical SLURM scheduling, and the dataset is already available on disk. The dataset used is synthetic generation because no real-world agricultural yield dataset with historical weather records and diverse crop types is available in the provided list of datasets.
experiment_plans.objective: To determine whether gradient-boosted models trained on historical weather records achieve higher seasonal crop yield prediction accuracy than a simple degree-day growth model when evaluated on a real-world agricultural dataset with diverse climatic conditions and crop types.
experiment_plans.design: Comparative benchmark experiment where we train two models (gradient-boosted model and degree-day model) on the same dataset and compare their performance using cross-validation.

data_requirements.description: Synthetic agricultural yield data generated to mimic real-world conditions with diverse crop types, climatic conditions, and historical weather records. This includes features like temperature, precipitation, humidity, and soil conditions, along with corresponding crop yield values.
preprocessing_steps: Generate synthetic dataset with realistic agricultural variables
Ensure diversity in crop types (e.g., wheat, corn, soybeans)
Include varied climatic conditions (temperature, precipitation, humidity)
Add historical weather records with appropriate temporal granularity
Create target variable representing crop yield in tons/hectare

methods.name: Machine Learning Models (Gradient Boosted Trees)
methods.description: A gradient-boosted model (specifically XGBoost) that learns complex non-linear relationships between weather variables and crop yields. Features include temperature, precipitation, humidity, and other climatic indicators. The model is trained to predict crop yield based on historical weather records.

methods.name: Glacio-hydrological Degree-day Model (GDM)
methods.description: A simple degree-day model that calculates crop growth based on accumulated temperature above a base threshold. This serves as the baseline model for comparison. It uses temperature data to estimate crop development stages and final yield.

evaluation.baseline: Degree-day model performance on the same dataset
evaluation.success_criteria: If the gradient-boosted model achieves lower MAE, RMSE, and higher R² scores compared to the degree-day model, the hypothesis is supported. If the degree-day model performs equally well or better, the hypothesis is refuted.

implementation_steps.description: Generate synthetic agricultural dataset with diverse crop types, climatic conditions, and historical weather records using Python libraries like NumPy and Pandas. Save as CSV file.
Load the synthetic dataset into memory using pandas.read_csv(). Split into training (80%) and testing (20%) sets while maintaining temporal order.
Preprocess the data by normalizing numerical features and encoding categorical variables (crop type). Create additional features like cumulative temperature and precipitation sums.
Train the XGBoost gradient-boosted model using scikit-learn's XGBRegressor with default parameters on the training set. Optimize hyperparameters using GridSearchCV if time allows.
Implement the degree-day model using basic temperature accumulation calculations. Calculate degree-days above a base temperature threshold for each crop type.
Evaluate both models on the test set using MAE, RMSE, and R² metrics. Store results in structured format for comparison.
Compare model performances using statistical significance tests (e.g., paired t-test) to determine if differences are meaningful.
Generate visualizations showing prediction accuracy for both models across different crop types and climatic conditions.

risks: Synthetic data might not accurately reflect real-world complexities
Model overfitting due to limited synthetic samples
Computational time for hyperparameter tuning if included
Potential bias in synthetic data generation leading to misleading conclusions
